1	# Automated RF Antenna Placement via AI Agent + EM Simulation: Research & System Specification
2	
3	*A grounding document for a hackathon team building software that uses an AI coding agent (Devin) to determine optimal antenna placement in a phone design (from a Blender 3D model), run electromagnetic simulations, and output engineering recommendations. Written so each teammate — 3D modeling, UI/visualization, simulation, agent integration — can extract what's relevant and begin immediately.*
4	
5	## TL;DR
6	- **Feasible with real caveats.** A team can build an end-to-end pipeline where an AI coding agent ingests a Blender phone model plus a device-constraint spec, generates and runs open-source FDTD electromagnetic simulations (openEMS), and outputs ranked antenna-placement recommendations — **but full-fidelity FDTD of a whole phone takes tens of minutes to hours per run**, so the demo must use coarse meshes, a small candidate set, and/or surrogate models. Do not promise "thousands of configurations."
7	- **Recommended stack:** Blender (geometry) → glTF/STL export with per-component material tags → Three.js viewer for the UI → **openEMS** (Python, GPLv3, free, fully scriptable, with a built-in SAR post-processor) as the solver → **Devin v3 API** orchestrating a simulate–evaluate–optimize loop with structured JSON output.
8	- **Core RF facts to build against:** phone antennas are electrically small resonators (PIFA/IFA/monopole/loop below 6 GHz, patch arrays at mmWave); target −6 to −10 dB S11, VSWR < 2–3, >40–50% efficiency; respect keep-out zones (≥15 mm clearance at 2.4 GHz, more at sub-GHz); SAR limits are **1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g of tissue (FCC, per 47 CFR §1.1310)** and **2.0 W/kg over 10 g (ICNIRP/CE)**.
9	
10	## Key Findings
11	1. **openEMS is the only realistic full-wave solver for this hackathon:** free, GPLv3, Python-scriptable, handles bulk dielectrics, computes S-parameters/near+far fields/radiation patterns, and includes built-in 1g/10g SAR averaging. A community MCP server (`mcp-openems` by RFingAdam) already generates complete openEMS Python scripts from AI agents.
12	2. **The Devin v3 API supports the full loop needed:** upload files → create a session with a structured-output JSON schema → send follow-up messages → poll status → download agent-produced artifacts.
13	3. **Whole-phone FDTD is the bottleneck.** A single moderately-meshed run is roughly an hour on a quad-core CPU; brute-force sweeps of hundreds of configs are infeasible without coarse models, parallelism, or ML surrogates.
14	4. **Placement is normally a manual, iterative RF-engineer task;** characteristic mode analysis (CMA) is the standard "where to place / where to feed" pre-simulation technique and is a good conceptual model for the agent's candidate-generation layer.
15	5. **Autonomous agent design loops already work in adjacent domains** (photonics, inertial fusion, turbomachinery, chip DSE), validating the architecture — e.g., an agentic photonics loop used an MCP interface to solvers plus a GPU cluster to run hundreds of simulations per design problem (Kharel et al., *Autonomous agentic design for photonics*, arXiv:2606.00915, 2026).
16	
17	## Details
18	
19	### 1. Phone/Mobile Antenna Fundamentals
20	
21	**How phone antennas work.** A phone antenna is a resonant conductor that converts guided RF currents into radiated EM waves. In handsets the antenna and the PCB ground plane together form the radiating system — the ground plane (chassis) is itself an essential radiator at low bands, which is why placement and clearance matter so much. Most handset antennas are "electrically small" (smaller than a quarter wavelength), which forces trade-offs between size, bandwidth, and efficiency.
22	
23	**Antenna types (comparison):**
24	
25	| Type | Typical bands | Size/profile | Bandwidth | Pros | Cons | Phone use |
26	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
27	| PIFA (Planar Inverted-F) | 0.7–6 GHz | Low profile, needs volume above ground | Moderate | Compact, low SAR, less hand-detuning | Needs height/clearance | Legacy main cellular |
28	| IFA (Inverted-F) | 0.7–6 GHz, 2.4/5 GHz | Very thin, PCB-etched | Narrow–moderate | Cheap, integrable on PCB | Narrow bandwidth | Wi-Fi/BT, secondary |
29	| Monopole / loop | 0.6–6 GHz | Small footprint | Moderate | Simple, wideband variants | Needs ground plane | Main + diversity |
30	| Metal-frame/bezel | 0.6–6 GHz | Uses the phone's metal rim | Wide (multi-mode) | Uses existing structure, ID-friendly | Complex tuning, hand effects | Modern flagships |
31	| Patch / microstrip | >2 GHz, mmWave | Planar on substrate | Narrow | Directional, array-able | Narrow BW, large at low freq | mmWave elements |
32	| Slot | Various | Cut in ground/frame | Moderate | Integrates into metal | Design complexity | Metal-frame phones |
33	| Ceramic chip | 2.4/5 GHz, GNSS | Tiny SMD | Narrow | Smallest, easy assembly | Lower efficiency | Wi-Fi/BT/GPS |
34	| Flexible/FPC | 0.6–6 GHz | Conforms to housing | Moderate | Fits curved housing | Assembly complexity | Cellular main in slim phones |
35	| mmWave array (AiP) | 24–40 GHz | Module, multiple elements | Wide | Beam steering, high gain | LOS-limited, blockage | 5G FR2 |
36	
37	*Real-world mmWave reference:* Qualcomm's QTM052 module integrates a phased array + transceiver + RF front-end, covers n257/n261/n260 (26.5–29.5, 27.5–28.35, 37–40 GHz), supports up to 800 MHz bandwidth, and up to four modules are placed in one phone for blockage resilience; face or edge placement give similar performance.
38	
39	**Frequency bands used in phones:**
40	
41	| Service | Frequency | Notes |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| Cellular low-band (LTE/5G FR1) | ~600–960 MHz (B71 600 MHz, B5 850, B8 900) | Best coverage/penetration; largest antenna & clearance |
44	| Cellular mid-band | ~1.7–2.7 GHz (B1, B3, B7) | Capacity/coverage balance |
45	| 5G NR sub-6 mid/high | 3.3–5.0 GHz (n77/n78/n79) | C-band; 100 MHz channels common |
46	| 5G mmWave (FR2) | 24–40 GHz (n257 26.5–29.5, n261 27.5–28.35, n260 37–40) | Phased arrays, beam steering, LOS |
47	| Wi-Fi | 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E/7) | |
48	| Bluetooth | 2.4 GHz ISM | Often shares Wi-Fi 2.4 antenna |
49	| GPS/GNSS | ~1.559–1.610 GHz (GPS L1 1575.42, GLONASS ~1602, Galileo/BeiDou) | Dedicated or shared |
50	| NFC | 13.56 MHz | Inductive loop, not a radiating antenna |
51	
52	**Performance metrics engineers care about:**
53	- **S11 / return loss** — reflection at the port; engineers target **S11 ≤ −6 dB (handsets) to −10 dB**. −10 dB return loss ≈ VSWR 2:1; −20 dB ≈ 1.2:1. (A VSWR of 3 reflects ~25% of incident power.)
54	- **VSWR** — impedance match; < 2 acceptable, < 1.5 excellent.
55	- **Bandwidth** — frequency range meeting the S11 threshold.
56	- **Gain (dBi)** and **radiation efficiency** — handset main antennas often run 40–60% total efficiency; above 50% is good given losses.
57	- **Radiation pattern** — near-omnidirectional desired for cellular; directional/steerable for mmWave.
58	- **Isolation** (S12/S21) between antennas — target better than −10 to −15 dB for MIMO/diversity; improved via spatial separation, decoupling structures, and ground-plane current control.
59	- **SAR** — regulatory tissue-absorption limit (see §6).
60	- **Detuning** — frequency shift from hand, head, battery, enclosure; a central design risk (S11 detuning worsens as air gap to tissue shrinks).
61	
62	**Placement constraints in real phones:**
63	- **Keep-out zones**: a 3D copper-free/component-free volume around the antenna, treated as a **hard constraint** from the antenna datasheet — "your schematic is a suggestion; your PCB layout is the law." Rule of thumb ~15 mm clearance for 2.4 GHz; larger at sub-GHz. No ground/power plane under the radiator on any layer. Even a single grounded mounting screw inside the zone can detune the antenna and fail RF testing.
64	- **Ground plane**: continuous, and large enough (≥ λ/4 in the relevant dimension; ~30 mm minimum for a 2.4 GHz quarter-wave monopole/IFA). Use edge stitching vias (< λ/10 spacing) but never inside the keep-out.
65	- **Placement at corners/edges** gives clearance in multiple directions; multiple antennas go in separate corners for isolation.
66	- **Avoid** battery, LCD/screen metal, cameras, shield cans, speakers, and high-speed switching noise near the antenna.
67	- **Enclosure material**: plastic is RF-transparent; glass is a moderate dielectric (εr ≈ 5.5) that loads/detunes (screen assemblies are commonly modeled as a ~2 mm glass layer, εr 5.5, or as a grounded metal plate for the worst case); metal backs/frames block RF and require non-conductive "antenna lines"/slots. A metal enclosure acts simultaneously as ground plane, reflector, shield, and resonant cavity.
68	
69	**How placement is chosen today.** It's a manual, iterative, experience-driven process: RF engineers pick antenna type and a corner/edge location from datasheet reference designs, use **characteristic mode analysis (CMA)** (in HFSS or CST) to understand chassis current modes and where to feed, then run full-wave simulation, tune a matching network, build, and measure in an anechoic chamber — iterating multiple times. CMA "gives physical insight of the current pattern... and helps as a first step toward achieving correct antenna placement." Tools: ANSYS HFSS, CST Studio Suite, FEKO for simulation; VNAs and chambers for measurement.
70	
71	### 2. Electromagnetic Simulation for Antenna Design
72	
73	**Numerical methods for Maxwell's equations:**
74	
75	| Method | Domain | Best for | Notes |
76	|---|---|---|---|
77	| FDTD (Finite-Difference Time-Domain) | Time | Broadband, transient, dielectrics, SAR | One run → wideband S-params; used by openEMS, Meep, XFdtd, CST time-domain |
78	| MoM (Method of Moments) | Frequency | Metal antennas, wires, planar | Efficient for conductors; NEC, FEKO, Momentum |
79	| FEM (Finite Element Method) | Frequency | Complex geometry, resonant | HFSS, COMSOL; adaptive meshing |
80	| FIT (Finite Integration Technique) | Time/freq | General 3D | CST's core method |
81	
82	**EM tool comparison (hackathon lens):**
83	
84	| Tool | Method | License | Scriptable/API | Learning curve | Hackathon feasibility |
85	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
86	| **openEMS** | EC-FDTD | Free, **GPLv3** | **Python + Octave/Matlab** | Medium | **Best choice** — free, automatable, MCP server exists, bulk dielectrics + SAR |
87	| Meep | FDTD | Free, open | Python/Scheme/C++ | Medium | Great but optics-oriented |
88	| NEC2 / 4nec2 | MoM | Free/open | Text decks | Low–med | Wire antennas only; no bulk dielectrics |
89	| Sonnet Lite | MoM | Free (limited) | Limited | Medium | Planar only |
90	| CST Studio Suite | FIT/FEM | Commercial (expensive) | Python/VBA macros | High | License barrier; has CMA tool |
91	| ANSYS HFSS | FEM (+ hybrid) | Commercial (expensive) | PyAEDT/Python | High | License barrier; has CMA tool |
92	| FEKO | MoM/MLFMM/hybrid | Commercial | Lua/API | High | License barrier; strong for electrically large |
93	| Antenna Magus | Synthesis DB | Commercial | Export to solvers | Low | Design starter, not a solver |
94	
95	**Recommendation: openEMS.** It is the only free, fully Python-scriptable full-wave solver that handles bulk dielectrics (essential to model FR4, glass, battery). Per the official docs (docs.openems.de), "openEMS is licensed under the GNU General Public License, Version 3 or later" and "simulations are defined via an extensive set of Matlab/Octave or Python interfaces," with built-in near-field-to-far-field transform, 1g/10g SAR calculation, and multi-threading/SIMD/MPI support. The **`mcp-openems`** MCP server (by RFingAdam, AGPL-3.0) exposes an `openems_generate_script` tool that "creates a complete Python script" for FDTD S-parameter/radiation-pattern simulation — a direct fit for agent orchestration.
96	
97	**Setting up a parametrized simulation:**
98	- **Geometry import**: openEMS geometry is defined in CSXCAD (primitives + polyhedra). Import Blender/CAD via STL/OBJ (mesh) or STEP (CAD). STL is simplest but lossy (triangles, no materials; Blender assumes meters if units are unset). STEP preserves solids/units/materials but needs a converter. Practical path: export each labeled Blender component as a separate STL/OBJ, then map each to an openEMS material in code.
99	- **Materials** (define εr and loss tangent):
100	  - PCB FR4: εr ≈ 4.3–4.7 (use **4.4**), tanδ ≈ 0.02 (lossy above ~4 GHz; note vendor/frequency spread of 3.9–4.8)
101	  - Metal (ground, frame, shields): PEC or finite-conductivity copper
102	  - Glass back/screen: εr ≈ 5.5
103	  - Plastic housing: εr ≈ 2.5–3, low loss
104	  - Battery: model as a lossy metal box / lossy dielectric block (conservative: treat as a PEC block for worst-case detuning)
105	- **Ports/feed**: lumped port at the antenna feed (typically 50 Ω); openEMS `calcPort` extracts S-parameters.
106	- **Mesh**: rule of thumb **λ/20** cell size at the highest frequency; refine at fine features (feed, thin traces) using the 1/3–2/3 rule; graded/smoothed mesh lines to limit cell count. openEMS does **not** auto-mesh fully — mesh lines must be specified (Python `automesh`/`SmoothMeshLines` helpers exist).
107	- **Boundary conditions**: MUR (simple absorbing) or PML (`PML_8`, better absorption), placed ~λ/2 from the structure; NF2FF box a few cells inside the boundary for the far-field transform. A Gaussian excitation with a center + corner frequency drives the broadband run; an end-criterion (e.g., −40 to −50 dB energy decay) stops it.
108	
109	**Candidate generation & optimization:**
110	- **Grid search** over discrete positions (corners/edges) × antenna types × lengths — simplest, agent-friendly, embarrassingly parallel.
111	- **Genetic algorithms / PSO** — classic for antenna geometry; needs many evaluations (e.g., parallel PSO/FDTD for multiband patches).
112	- **Bayesian optimization** — sample-efficient, ideal when each sim is expensive (the hackathon case).
113	- **Surrogate models** — train kriging/GP/neural nets on a handful of EM runs, then optimize on the cheap surrogate; literature reports reaching global optima in as few as ~120 high-fidelity EM simulations, and surrogate-assisted searches needing only tens of true EM validations (e.g., ~44 HFSS validations after a 2000-evaluation surrogate search).
114	
115	**Compute/runtime reality:**
116	- A single moderately-detailed openEMS antenna run is **roughly an hour on a quad-core i7**; simpler tutorial antennas run in minutes. An FDTD breast-phantom study cited ~10 hours on 8 cores. Runtime is driven by mesh density (fine features + high frequencies) and the ≥ λ/2 bounding box.
117	- Running "hundreds/thousands" of full-fidelity configs in a hackathon is **not feasible**. **Shortcuts:** coarse mesh (λ/10), reduced frequency band, 2D/quasi-static pre-screening, CMA to prune positions before simulating, aggressive parallelism (openEMS multithreading/MPI/GPU), and ML surrogates. Realistic demo target: **5–20 candidate configs** at coarse mesh, or a surrogate trained on ~10–30 runs.
118	
119	### 3. AI Coding Agent Orchestration (Devin v3 API)
120	
121	**Devin API basics.** REST API, base URL `https://api.devin.ai/v3`, Bearer auth with a service-user key (`cog_` prefix; v1 used `apk_*`). Core capabilities: Devin plans, writes/edits code, runs shell commands, reads docs/browses the web, self-heals failing code, and returns validated structured output. Usage is metered in **ACUs (Agent Compute Units)** — per Cognition's own definition, "a normalized measure of the computing resources Devin uses to complete a task, such as virtual machine time, model inference, and networking bandwidth," where "1 ACU works out to about 15 minutes of Devin actively working." ACUs are not consumed while a session sleeps; cap per session via `max_acu_limit`. (Note: Cognition's public self-serve pricing has shifted toward daily/weekly dollar quotas — Free / Pro $20 / Max $200 / Teams — so treat exact ACU prices as time-sensitive and verify against live docs.)
122	
123	**Endpoint cheat sheet (verified against docs.devin.ai):**
124	
125	| Purpose | Method + Path |
126	|---|---|
127	| Upload file → get URL | `POST /v1/attachments` (multipart form field **`file`**; returns the attachment URL as a plain string) |
128	| Create session | `POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions` — body `{prompt (required), attachment_urls[], repos[], max_acu_limit, structured_output_schema, structured_output_required, devin_mode}` |
129	| Follow-up message | `POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions/{devin_id}/messages` — `{"message": "..."}` (auto-resumes a suspended session) |
130	| Poll messages/events | `GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions/{devin_id}/messages` (cursor-paginated; items have `source: devin|user`) |
131	| Poll status | `GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions/{devin_id}` (read `status`, `status_detail`, `structured_output`, `acus_consumed`) |
132	| List output artifacts | `GET /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions/{devin_id}/attachments` (each item: `attachment_id`, `name`, `url`, `source`, `content_type`; filter `source == "devin"`) |
133	| Download artifact | HTTP GET the `url` field of each attachment (pre-signed URL; no separate download endpoint) |
134	
135	**Key mechanics for the build:**
136	- **Files IN:** upload via `POST /v1/attachments` to get a URL, then either pass URLs in `attachment_urls[]` on create-session **or** embed them in the prompt using the exact literal format **`ATTACHMENT:"{file_url}"`** — all caps, singular, on its own line (the plural `ATTACHMENTS:` is NOT recognized). Alternatively link a GitHub repo via the `repos[]` array. `devin_id` = `session_id` with the `devin-` prefix.
137	- **Status enum:** `new, claimed, running, exit, error, suspended, resuming`. Poll until `status` ∈ `(exit, error, suspended)` or `status_detail == "finished"`. `status_detail` while running: `working, waiting_for_user, waiting_for_approval, finished`.
138	- **Files OUT / results:** the cleanest machine-readable path is **structured output** — define a JSON Schema (Draft 7, ≤ 64 KB, self-contained) at create-time via `structured_output_schema`; Devin validates and updates `structured_output` as it works (tell it to update "whenever something relevant happens"). Generated files (openEMS scripts, result plots, the final report) come back through the attachments endpoint. Handle both a bare-array and an `{"items":[...]}` wrapper on the attachments response, as the docs are inconsistent.
139	
140	**Agentic loop architecture (simulate–evaluate–optimize):**
141	1. **Orchestrator** (your code, or Devin itself) reads the device-constraint spec + Blender export.
142	2. **Candidate generation**: agent proposes N placements/types (grid or CMA-informed).
143	3. **Simulation tool**: agent writes/edits an openEMS Python script per candidate and runs it in its VM (or calls an exposed simulator tool / `mcp-openems`).
144	4. **Evaluation**: agent parses S11/efficiency/pattern, checks against requirements, updates structured output.
145	5. **Iterate**: agent selects next candidates (Bayesian/surrogate) until an ACU/time budget or the acceptance thresholds are met.
146	6. **Report**: agent emits the final ranked recommendation + artifacts.
147	
148	Define tool-calling interfaces cleanly: `run_simulation(config) -> results.json`, `read_geometry(file) -> parts[]`, and `check_keepout(config) -> bool`. MCP servers (openEMS) are the natural integration surface.
149	
150	**Precedent.** Autonomous agent design loops are demonstrated in photonics (Kharel et al., arXiv:2606.00915 — "a model context protocol (MCP) interface for tighter agent integration with the simulation tools (Tidy3D, PhotonForge), an in-house GPU cluster that lets the agent run hundreds of simulations per design problem"), inertial-fusion multiphysics (arXiv:2510.17830), turbomachinery aerodynamics (TurboAgent), and chip design-space exploration (gem5 Co-Pilot) — all validating an LLM-driven perceive–reason–act loop over a scriptable solver.
151	
152	### 4. 3D Model / Blender Integration
153	
154	**Representing components for EM.** Model PCB, ground plane, enclosure, battery, camera, and the antenna candidate region as **separate, named Blender objects/collections**, each assigned a material that maps to EM properties (εr, tanδ, conductivity). Keep meshes watertight and low-poly (EM meshing re-discretizes anyway; excessive triangles slow import). Set Blender scene units explicitly to **mm**, since STL carries no unit metadata (Blender assumes meters otherwise).
155	
156	**Export formats:**
157	- **STL** — simplest; triangles only, one object per file recommended (batch-export add-ons exist); no materials → map materials by filename in code.
158	- **OBJ** — carries material *names* via an accompanying MTL file, useful for labeling.
159	- **glTF/GLB** — best for the UI viewer (below); packs meshes + PBR materials into one file.
160	- **STEP** — preserves solids/units/materials; importing to Blender needs an add-on (Cascadio/glTF pipeline, or SimLab which preserves materials). Good for CAD interchange but heavier; STEP export from Blender is generally not supported (mesh → B-Rep is lossy).
161	
162	**UI visualization with ray tracing + labeled components.** Export glTF/GLB from Blender → render in a **Three.js WebGL viewer** (`GLTFLoader`). For ray tracing, use a Three.js GPU path-tracing renderer (e.g., erichlof's THREE.js-PathTracing-Renderer, which supports glTF models with PBR albedo/emissive/metallic-roughness/normal maps). Use the Three.js **raycaster** for click-to-select/label components (map mesh `name` → component labels/textures/keep-out overlays). Alternative: script Blender's Python API (`bpy`) to render labeled Cycles/EEVEE images and embed them. USD is an option for richer scene interchange.
163	
164	### 5. Software Architecture & Specifications
165	
166	**System architecture (in words):**
167	- **Input layer**: device-constraint spec (JSON), Blender model export (glTF for UI; STL/OBJ per-part for sim), requirements (bands, targets, regulatory).
168	- **Analysis layer**: parse geometry, detect keep-out zones and metal/ground regions, identify candidate placement surfaces.
169	- **Candidate generation layer**: enumerate {position, antenna type, dimensions} — grid or CMA-informed.
170	- **Simulation orchestration layer** (agent-driven): Devin writes/runs openEMS per candidate, parses results.
171	- **Ranking/optimization layer**: score candidates against requirements; Bayesian/surrogate loop.
172	- **Output/reporting layer**: ranked recommendations + rationale + artifacts, surfaced in the UI.
173	
174	**Data schemas (proposed contracts between teammates):**
175	
176	*Device constraint spec:*
177	```json
178	{
179	  "device_id": "phone_v1",
180	  "board": {"size_mm": [150, 70, 8], "stackup": "FR4", "epsilon_r": 4.4, "loss_tangent": 0.02},
181	  "enclosure": {"back": "glass", "frame": "aluminum", "epsilon_r_back": 5.5},
182	  "components": [
183	    {"name": "battery", "type": "lossy_metal", "bbox_mm": [[10,10,0],[80,60,4]]},
184	    {"name": "camera",  "type": "metal",       "bbox_mm": [[120,50,0],[145,68,5]]}
185	  ],
186	  "keepout_zones": [{"bbox_mm": [[0,0,0],[15,70,8]]}],
187	  "requirements": {
188	    "bands": [{"name":"n78","f_low_ghz":3.3,"f_high_ghz":3.8}],
189	    "s11_db_max": -6.0, "efficiency_min": 0.5, "vswr_max": 3.0,
190	    "sar_limit": {"standard":"FCC","w_per_kg":1.6,"mass_g":1}
191	  }
192	}
193	```
194	
195	*Candidate configuration:*
196	```json
197	{"candidate_id":"c001","position_mm":[5,35,4],"antenna_type":"IFA",
198	 "orientation":"edge","length_mm":26,"feed_point_mm":[5,33,4],"target_band":"n78"}
199	```
200	
201	*Simulation result:*
202	```json
203	{"candidate_id":"c001","status":"complete","runtime_s":2400,
204	 "s11_db":{"3.3":-4.1,"3.5":-11.2,"3.8":-6.0},
205	 "resonant_ghz":3.52,"bandwidth_mhz":180,"efficiency":0.57,"peak_gain_dbi":2.6,
206	 "meets_requirements":true,"notes":"−10 dB BW covers n78 mid"}
207	```
208	
209	This last object is also a good shape for Devin's `structured_output_schema` so results return machine-readable.
210	
211	**Sample end-to-end agent interaction.** User asks: *"Where should the antenna go in this phone, what type, what frequency, and what's the expected performance?"* The agent should:
212	1. Read the constraint spec + geometry; summarize board size, metal/keep-out regions, target bands.
213	2. Reason from RF principles: pick antenna type by band (IFA/monopole for sub-6, patch array for mmWave) and candidate corners/edges with maximum clearance.
214	3. Generate candidates; write an openEMS script per candidate.
215	4. Run coarse simulations (parallel where possible); parse S11/efficiency.
216	5. Rank; if none meet requirements, adjust length/matching and re-run (bounded by the ACU budget).
217	6. Emit structured output + a human-readable report.
218	
219	**Final engineering report contents:**
220	- Recommended antenna position (coordinates/region) + type + target band(s).
221	- Required keep-out region (3D volume).
222	- Matching-network starting values (e.g., an L/C π-network seed derived from the simulated port impedance).
223	- Simulation results summary (S11 plot data, efficiency, gain, radiation pattern, resonance/bandwidth).
224	- Design rationale (why this position/type; CMA/clearance reasoning).
225	- Comparison against requirements (pass/fail per metric) and ranked runner-up options.
226	- Risks/caveats (hand/head detuning, SAR exposure, fabrication tolerance).
227	
228	### 6. Regulatory and Practical Constraints
229	- **SAR limits**: **FCC/ISED (US/Canada): 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g** of tissue — per the FCC RF-safety guidance ("The safe limit for a mobile phone user is an SAR of 1.6 watts per kg (1.6 W/kg), averaged over one gram of tissue") and codified in **47 CFR §1.1310**. **CE/ICNIRP (EU): 2.0 W/kg averaged over 10 g** (ICNIRP 2020 retains the ICNIRP 1998 value, averaged over a 10-g cubic region). **Extremity limit: 4 W/kg over 10 g** (hands, wrists, feet, ankles, pinnae — 47 CFR §1.1310). FCC's 1-g averaging is functionally stricter than the EU's 10-g averaging. The **combined SAR** of simultaneous transmitters at the same body location must stay under the limit.
230	- **Testing/exemptions**: portable devices with antennas within **20 cm of the body** must demonstrate SAR compliance via standardized phantom testing (FCC OET **KDB 447498**); low-power devices may be categorically excluded, but thresholds are tight (especially Bluetooth at close body separation). SAR testing commonly runs several thousand dollars and can force a redesign, so it belongs in the input spec from day one.
231	- **Certification basics**: FCC equipment authorization (US), CE/RED (EU), ISED (Canada); mmWave has additional regional rules. EIRP and MPE (maximum permissible exposure) limits also apply.
232	- **As an input parameter**, "regulatory constraints" should include: target markets, applicable SAR standard + averaging mass, body-separation distance, simultaneous-transmission scenarios, and per-band EIRP limits.
233	
234	## Recommendations
235	**Stage 0 — Scope the demo (hour 0–2).** Fix ONE target band (e.g., n78 3.3–3.8 GHz or Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz) and ONE antenna type (IFA or monopole) to bound the problem. Freeze the JSON schemas above as the contracts between teammates so all four workstreams proceed in parallel immediately.
236	
237	**Stage 1 — Parallel workstreams.**
238	- *3D modeler*: build the phone as separate named components (PCB, ground, battery, camera, enclosure, antenna-region), units in mm; export glTF (UI) + per-part STL (sim). Ship a fixture STL early so the sim person can start.
239	- *UI/viz*: Three.js + `GLTFLoader` viewer, raycaster click-to-label, optional GPU path tracer; overlay keep-out zones and candidate positions.
240	- *Sim*: get openEMS running an IFA/patch-on-ground-plane tutorial first; wrap it as `run_simulation(config) -> result.json`; validate against a known result before integrating.
241	- *Agent*: stand up the Devin v3 flow (upload → create with `structured_output_schema` → poll → download artifacts); test with a trivial "generate and run an openEMS script" task and confirm the `ATTACHMENT:"{url}"` format works.
242	
243	**Stage 2 — Integrate the loop (mid-hackathon).** Wire candidate generation (grid of 5–20 positions) → agent runs coarse openEMS (λ/10 mesh, single band) → rank by S11/efficiency → structured output → UI. Keep each sim under ~5–10 min by coarsening the mesh and shrinking the box.
244	
245	**Stage 3 — If time permits.** Add a surrogate model (GP over a handful of runs) or Bayesian optimization to cut simulation count; add SAR post-processing (openEMS built-in); seed a matching network from the simulated impedance.
246	
247	**Benchmarks that change the plan:** if a single coarse sim exceeds ~10 min, cut mesh resolution or candidate count, or switch to a 2D/quasi-static pre-screen; if openEMS setup stalls past hour 4, fall back to NEC2 for a wire-monopole proof, or feed pre-computed results to the agent/UI so the demo still shows the full pipeline end to end.
248	
249	## Caveats
250	- **Runtime is the dominant risk.** Full-wave FDTD of a whole phone is slow; the demo must use coarse models, few candidates, or surrogates.
251	- **Geometry fidelity vs. speed.** Highly detailed Blender meshes slow EM import/meshing; simplify to RF-relevant conductors and bulk dielectrics.
252	- **Material values are approximate.** FR4 εr varies 3.9–4.8 with frequency/vendor; battery/screen models are simplifications. Results are directional, not certification-grade.
253	- **openEMS has no full auto-mesher** and a not-fully-complete Python interface for some features — budget setup time.
254	- **Devin specifics may shift.** API pricing/ACU rates and some endpoint response wrappers are in flux; verify against live docs and handle both bare-array and `{"items":[...]}` attachment responses. Concurrent-session caps and rate limits (HTTP 429) apply — back off and retry.
255	- **Simulation ≠ measurement.** Real hand/head detuning and SAR require physical testing; the tool guides design, it does not replace the anechoic chamber or certification lab.
256	- **Source quality note.** Primary RF facts (openEMS behavior, Devin docs, FCC/ICNIRP SAR limits, mmWave module specs, agent-loop precedents) are drawn from authoritative sources (openEMS/Devin official docs, FCC/eCFR, IEEE/arXiv, Qualcomm/Microwave Journal). Some tool-comparison and PCB-guideline details come from vendor blogs and buyer's guides and are lower-authority — corroborate before making irreversible design decisions.

1	"""Scoring + diagnosis: turn SimResults into the evidence layers the agent
2	reasons over (DESIGN.md §6.4). Hints are deterministic physics arithmetic —
3	never LLM output. The scalar score exists for ranking/UI only."""
4	from __future__ import annotations
5	
6	from app.geometry.spec import clearance_at
7	from app.models import (BandRequirement, Candidate, CandidateReport,
8	                        DeviceSpec, IterationReport, RequirementDiff, SimResult)
9	
10	
11	def diffs_for(spec: DeviceSpec, band: BandRequirement, cand: Candidate,
12	              r: SimResult) -> list[RequirementDiff]:
13	    in_band = [p for p in r.s11_curve
14	               if band.f_low_ghz <= p.f_ghz <= band.f_high_ghz]
15	    worst = max((p.s11_db for p in in_band), default=0.0)
16	    clear_mm, _blocker = clearance_at(spec, cand.position_mm)
17	    band_mhz = (band.f_high_ghz - band.f_low_ghz) * 1000.0
18	    return [
19	        RequirementDiff(requirement="worst in-band S11", target=band.s11_db_max,
20	                        actual=round(worst, 2), margin=round(band.s11_db_max - worst, 2),
21	                        unit="dB", passing=worst <= band.s11_db_max),
22	        RequirementDiff(requirement="-6 dB bandwidth covers band", target=band_mhz,
23	                        actual=r.bandwidth_mhz, margin=round(r.bandwidth_mhz - band_mhz, 1),
24	                        unit="MHz", passing=r.bandwidth_mhz >= band_mhz),
25	        RequirementDiff(requirement="total efficiency", target=band.efficiency_min,
26	                        actual=r.efficiency, margin=round(r.efficiency - band.efficiency_min, 3),
27	                        unit="", passing=r.efficiency >= band.efficiency_min),
28	        RequirementDiff(requirement="VSWR", target=spec.requirements.vswr_max,
29	                        actual=r.vswr, margin=round(spec.requirements.vswr_max - r.vswr, 2),
30	                        unit="", passing=r.vswr <= spec.requirements.vswr_max),
31	        RequirementDiff(requirement="clearance to nearest metal", target=band.clearance_mm,
32	                        actual=round(clear_mm, 1), margin=round(clear_mm - band.clearance_mm, 1),
33	                        unit="mm", passing=clear_mm >= band.clearance_mm),
34	    ]
35	
36	
37	def hints_for(spec: DeviceSpec, band: BandRequirement, cand: Candidate,
38	              r: SimResult) -> list[str]:
39	    hints: list[str] = []
40	    if r.status != "complete":
41	        return [f"simulation failed: {r.notes}"]
42	    f_t = band.f_mid_ghz
43	    f_lo_sweep = r.s11_curve[0].f_ghz
44	    f_hi_sweep = r.s11_curve[-1].f_ghz
45	
46	    if abs(r.resonant_ghz - f_lo_sweep) < 1e-6 or abs(r.resonant_ghz - f_hi_sweep) < 1e-6:
47	        hints.append(
48	            f"resonance pinned at sweep edge ({r.resonant_ghz:.2f} GHz) — true "
49	            f"resonance likely outside window; change length_mm decisively")
50	    elif abs(r.resonant_ghz - f_t) / f_t > 0.015:
51	        scale = r.resonant_ghz / f_t
52	        hints.append(
53	            f"resonance {r.resonant_ghz:.2f} GHz vs target {f_t:.2f} → element "
54	            f"{'short' if scale > 1 else 'long'} by ~{abs(scale-1)*100:.0f}%; "
55	            f"try length_mm ≈ {cand.length_mm * scale:.1f}")
56	
57	    R, X = r.impedance_ohm
58	    if R == 0 and X == 0:
59	        pass  # solver reported no input impedance (external engines) — no R hints
60	    elif R < 20:
61	        fix = ("increase gap_mm (moves feed tap up the impedance curve)"
62	               if cand.antenna_type == "IFA"
63	               else "consider IFA — a shorting post transforms low R upward")
64	        hints.append(f"radiation resistance low (R={R:.0f} Ω vs 50) → {fix}")
65	    elif R > 110:
66	        if cand.antenna_type == "IFA":
67	            hints.append(f"R={R:.0f} Ω too high → decrease gap_mm")
68	
69	    clear_mm, blocker = clearance_at(spec, cand.position_mm)
70	    if clear_mm < band.clearance_mm:
71	        hints.append(
72	            f"keep-out violated: {clear_mm:.1f} mm to {blocker} "
73	            f"(need ≥ {band.clearance_mm:.0f}) — detuning risk; prefer another anchor")
74	
75	    if r.bandwidth_mhz == 0 and -6.0 < r.s11_min_db <= -4.0:
76	        hints.append("match is marginal, not absent — small length/gap moves may cross -6 dB")
77	    return hints
78	
79	
80	def score_of(diffs: list[RequirementDiff]) -> float:
81	    s = 0.5
82	    for d in diffs:
83	        if d.requirement == "worst in-band S11":
84	            s += max(min(0.08 * d.margin, 0.3), -0.3)
85	        elif d.requirement == "total efficiency":
86	            s += max(min(0.5 * d.margin, 0.1), -0.1)
87	        elif d.requirement == "clearance to nearest metal":
88	            s += max(min(0.03 * d.margin, 0.1), -0.15)
89	        elif d.requirement == "-6 dB bandwidth covers band":
90	            s += 0.05 if d.passing else -0.05
91	    return round(max(0.0, min(1.0, s)), 3)
92	
93	
94	def build_report(spec: DeviceSpec, band_for, iteration: int,
95	                 cands: dict[str, Candidate], results: dict[str, SimResult],
96	                 history_best: list[float]) -> IterationReport:
97	    """`band_for(candidate) -> BandRequirement` resolves each candidate's own
98	    band (multi-band runs score per band; ranking is by scalar score)."""
99	    reports: list[CandidateReport] = []
100	    for cid, r in results.items():
101	        cand = cands[cid]
102	        band = band_for(cand)
103	        ds = diffs_for(spec, band, cand, r) if r.status == "complete" else []
104	        reports.append(CandidateReport(
105	            candidate_id=cid, result=r, diffs=ds,
106	            score=score_of(ds) if ds else 0.0,
107	            hints=hints_for(spec, band, cand, r)))
108	    reports.sort(key=lambda cr: cr.score, reverse=True)
109	    best = reports[0].candidate_id if reports else None
110	
111	    trend = "first_iteration"
112	    if history_best:
113	        prev = history_best[-1]
114	        cur = reports[0].score if reports else 0.0
115	        if cur > prev + 0.02:
116	            trend = "converging"
117	        elif cur < prev - 0.02:
118	            trend = "regressing"
119	        else:
120	            trend = "plateaued"
121	    return IterationReport(iteration=iteration, reports=reports,
122	                           best_so_far=best, trend=trend)

# Wiring Devin (backend) to the real RF simulation — integration plan

> Draft for review, 2026-08-22 (rev. 2). Nothing here is implemented yet;
> this is the plan to review before code changes start. Once approved,
> execute §8 in order and check items off in place.

## 1. Where things actually stand

Both sides are individually done, but never run **together for real**:

- `rf/run_simulation(config: dict) -> dict` runs a genuine openEMS FDTD solve
  (IFA-over-ground-plane, optional real device dielectrics via
  `device.manifest_path`). Verified end-to-end on a demo candidate and on the
  real iPhone 15 Pro asset (bbox-approximated materials). **Not yet**
  cross-checked against a known-good resonance (tutorial / PyNEC oracle) —
  see `rf/progress_simulation.md` steps 2 and 4.
- The backend already has an adapter for it: `backend/app/sim/rf_adapter.py`
  maps backend `Candidate`/`DeviceSpec`/`BandRequirement` → rf's config dict
  and rf's result dict → backend `SimResult`. Selecting it is one env var:
  `SIM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve`.
- `backend/scripts/selftest.py::test_rf_adapter` only exercises this against
  a **stubbed** `rf.run_simulation` (a lambda injected into `sys.modules`).
  The adapter has never actually called the real openEMS solver.
- The **placement-search loop already exists and already works** — with the
  bundled fast oracle, not with rf's real solver. See §2.

So "connect the agent to the simulation" is really two separable things:
(a) make the already-written adapter work against the real solver (§3-5,
§8), and (b) make sure the agent still gets to *search* rather than grade a
single hand-picked spot once that real solver is slow (§6-7). The gap is
narrower than it looks, but both parts are real.

## 2. Does the pipeline actually search for a placement, or just grade one?

This came up directly, so it's worth being precise about the answer, because
it's "no" for one layer and "yes" for another:

- **`rf/run_simulation()` in isolation: no search, by design.** It is a pure
  function — one `Candidate` (one position, one length, one orientation) in,
  one `SimResult` out. Running `python -m rf.run_simulation` demos exactly
  one hand-typed position. **This is intentional** — `rf/` is the *grader*,
  not the *search*. Conflating the two would duplicate the anchor logic the
  backend already owns and couple the sim workstream to backend concerns.
- **The backend + agent loop around it: yes, this is where the search
  lives**, and it has already run and worked (against the bundled oracle):
  - `app/geometry/spec.py::make_anchors()` generates a **grid of candidate
    positions** around the device perimeter (4 corners + edge points at a
    configurable spacing) — this *is* the "candidate generation layer" from
    `deep_research_on_challenge.md` §5 ("grid search over discrete positions
    — simplest, agent-friendest, embarrassingly parallel").
  - Devin is hard-required to reason from *evidence*, not guess in a vacuum:
    each anchor comes with a computed `clearance_mm` (distance to the
    nearest metal obstacle — battery, camera, speaker, shield can), so the
    agent already knows which spots are physically promising before
    simulating any of them.
  - The agent proposes `simulate` batches across many anchors, then `sweep`s
    `length_mm`/`gap_mm` on the promising ones (§6.3 wire protocol) — this
    **is** the AI agent taking over the manual iterate-and-measure loop an
    RF engineer does by hand. It is not a stub: DESIGN.md records a live run
    (M2, real iPhone 15 Pro asset) where Devin tried multiple anchors across
    3 iterations / 32 simulations and picked a 28 mm corner monopole,
    rejecting the IFA family *on evidence*.
  - **What has not been tested:** doing this same breadth-first anchor
    search with the real, ~2-min-per-solve openEMS engine instead of the
    millisecond-per-solve bundled oracle. That's a real, new problem — not
    "no search exists," but "the existing search doesn't fit the real
    solver's budget yet." See §6.

**Plain-English recap, for anyone not deep in the RF weeds:** think of the
antenna as a piece of bent wire on the edge of the phone. `rf/`'s job is:
*given exactly one spot, one length, one shape — tell me how well that one
guess would actually work* (does it "resonate" at the right radio frequency,
does it waste power, does it match the electronics feeding it). It runs a
detailed, slow physics simulation (like ray-tracing for radio waves instead
of light) — good at grading, bad at guessing on its own. The backend is what
generates the *guesses* — it walks around the edge of the phone and drops
pins at each corner and every ~18 mm along the sides, checks which pins are
safely far from metal parts (battery, camera, speakers), and hands Devin
that list. Devin (told "try a batch, look at the numbers, try more, sweep
lengths, then decide") behaves like the human RF engineer who normally sits
there for days trying spot after spot — it just does it by reading numbers
back from `rf/` instead of soldering and re-measuring in a lab.

## 3. The actual blocker: two incompatible Python environments

- The backend runs on **Python 3.12** (`backend/pyproject.toml`,
  `requires-python = ">=3.12"`), managed by `uv`.
- openEMS/CSXCAD are prebuilt **Windows wheels for Python 3.11**, installed
  only inside `rf/.venv` (see `rf/README.md` Setup). They are not, and
  cannot be, installed into the backend's own venv (ABI mismatch).
- `rf_adapter.solve()` today does this **in-process**:
  ```python
  sys.path.insert(0, str(REPO_DIR))
  from rf.run_simulation import run_simulation   # imports openEMS transitively
  ```
- `app/sim/pool.py` runs `solve()` inside a `ProcessPoolExecutor` — but those
  worker processes are spawned from **the same interpreter as the backend**
  (Python 3.12, no openEMS). The import will fail with `ModuleNotFoundError`
  the moment `SIM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve` is set on a normal
  `uv run uvicorn ...` backend.

This is the *same* problem the backend already solved once, for `bpy`
(Blender's Python API, also version-pinned): `app/geometry/extract.py`
resolves a separate interpreter (`BPY_PYTHON` / `BLENDER` / ephemeral
`uv run --with bpy`) and shells out via `subprocess.run`, rather than
importing `bpy` in-process. `rf_adapter` needs the same treatment.

## 4. Backend structure, oriented at this integration

```
backend/app/
├── main.py               FastAPI app; lifespan starts/stops the sim process pool
├── api/routes.py          HTTP/WS surface: /runs, /devices, /runs/{id}/events
├── models.py              Pydantic mirror of frontend/src/lib/types.ts —
│                          DeviceSpec, Candidate, SimResult, the agent wire
│                          protocol (SimulateRequest/SweepRequest/DoneRequest/
│                          SpecRequest = AgentRequest union)
├── agent/
│   ├── port.py            AgentPort protocol — the ONE seam between the
│   │                      orchestrator and any agent implementation
│   ├── devin.py           Devin v3 client implementing AgentPort (see §5)
│   ├── mock.py            heuristic drop-in implementing the same protocol
│   └── prompts.py         builds the create-session prompt + per-iteration
│                          evidence messages; defines the fenced-JSON protocol
│                          text Devin is told to follow; ANTENNA_NOTES = the
│                          narrative engineering rules of thumb (see §7)
├── runs/
│   ├── orchestrator.py    the state machine — THE file that drives a run:
│   │                      services one agent action at a time, enforces the
│   │                      "no unsimulated done" gate, emits every event
│   ├── devices.py         .blend ingest → extraction → DeviceSpec lifecycle
│   ├── events.py, store.py  append-only per-run event log; in-memory registries
│   └── report.py          renders report.md / run.json / S11 CSV artifacts
├── geometry/
│   ├── extract.py         subprocess dispatch to a bpy-capable interpreter
│   │                      (THE PATTERN §8 reuses for rf)
│   ├── classify.py        geometry.json → DeviceSpec (EmClass, roles, ground)
│   ├── spec.py            canned phone_v1 + make_anchors() (the position
│   │                      grid, §2) + clearance_at() (hard-constraint check)
│   └── bands.py           band catalogue (mirrors frontend/src/lib/device.ts)
└── sim/
    ├── pool.py             ProcessPoolExecutor wrapper; resolves SIM_SOLVER
    │                       and calls `solve(spec, band, cand) -> SimResult`
    ├── oracle.py            bundled reference solver (PyNEC MoM) — default;
    │                       the fast solver the in-loop search should keep using
    ├── rf_adapter.py         <-- what this plan changes; maps to rf/run_simulation;
    │                       the slow/real solver — see §6 for how it's used
    ├── builders/            oracle's own antenna geometry builders (IFA, monopole)
    └── score.py              turns SimResult(s) into the evidence layers
                               (diff/trend/hint) the agent reasons over —
                               hints_for() = the deterministic-physics rules (§7)
```

**The one seam this plan touches:** `solve(spec, band, cand) -> SimResult` in
`app/sim/rf_adapter.py`, selected by `SIM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve`.
Nothing in `orchestrator.py`, `pool.py`, `score.py`, or the agent layer needs
to change for the adapter fix itself — that's the point of the seam. §6 adds
one small, separate seam (a confirmation call), described there.

## 5. How Devin actually "calls tools" (brief)

Devin does **not** use a function-calling / native tool-use API the way the
Anthropic Messages API does. There is no schema the backend registers with
Devin that Devin then invokes structurally. Instead:

1. The backend creates one Devin **session** per run (`POST /v3/.../sessions`)
   and sends a big **prompt** (`app/agent/prompts.py`) that includes a
   `## Protocol` section written in plain English + example JSON: *"each of
   your replies must contain exactly one fenced ```json block with ONE
   action: simulate | sweep | done | spec"*.
2. Devin runs autonomously **inside its own VM** — its own shell, filesystem,
   package manager. It can `pip install bpy`, run scripts, read an attached
   `.blend` file, and (if `repos: [...]` is set and the org's GitHub
   integration can see the repo) follow **Skills** — `SKILL.md` files under
   `.agents/skills/` that are auto-discovered and inject procedure ("run
   `tools/extract_blend.py` like this"). None of that VM-internal activity
   (shell commands, file edits) is visible to the backend as structured
   events — it's opaque compute happening on Devin's side.
3. The only thing the backend ever sees is **chat messages** Devin posts
   back into the session, fetched by polling
   `GET /sessions/{id}/messages?after={cursor}` every ~10-30 s
   (`DevinAgent._poll_messages` in `app/agent/devin.py`). Devin has no
   webhooks; this is deliberate, documented API design on their side.
4. `DevinAgent._parse_action` takes the **last fenced ```json block** in each
   new Devin-authored message, JSON-decodes it, and validates it against the
   `AgentRequest` Pydantic union in `app/models.py`. **That fenced block is
   the "tool call"** from the orchestrator's point of view — a
   backend-defined wire protocol carried inside ordinary chat text, not a
   native Devin tool-calling mechanism. Malformed JSON gets one corrective
   message ("your last reply had no valid action...") before falling back.
5. `orchestrator.py` executes the parsed action (run FDTD/PyNEC sims in the
   process pool, score them, build the evidence report) and sends the result
   back as the **next** chat message (`prompts.report_message`). Devin reads
   that evidence and replies with its next action. This request/response
   loop repeats until a `done` action passes the simulation gate.
6. Because `AgentPort` (`app/agent/port.py`) is the same narrow interface for
   both `DevinAgent` and the heuristic `MockAgent`, `orchestrator.py` never
   has agent-vendor-specific code in it — it just calls `next_action(report)`
   and gets back one of `SimulateRequest | SweepRequest | DoneRequest |
   SpecRequest`.

In short: **Devin's "tools" are backend concepts described in a prompt, not
API-registered functions** — the fenced-JSON convention *is* the tool-calling
layer, implemented entirely in our parsing code, not Devin's.

## 6. Letting the agent search *and* use the real solver (the actual conflict)

Wiring `SIM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve` naively makes the search in §2
run at real-FDTD speed: ~2 minutes/candidate instead of milliseconds. A full
anchor sweep (4 corners + edges every 18 mm — ~16-20 anchors for a phone-size
device) would take **30-60+ minutes** just for one pass, before any
`length_mm`/`gap_mm` sweep on top. Against `MAX_WALL_CLOCK_S = 8 * 60` in
`orchestrator.py`, that barrier trips after 3-4 candidates total — nowhere
near enough breadth for the agent to actually "take over the manual testing"
the way it already does with the fast oracle.

Cranking `MAX_WALL_CLOCK_S` way up "fixes" this but throws away exactly the
property that makes the demo watchable and the loop cheap. **Better fix,
already implied by the project's own architecture** (DESIGN.md ADR-3: *"PyNEC
in-loop... openEMS demoted to optional confirmation"*; M4 backlog already
names, as not yet built, *"openEMS single-shot confirmation of the
winner"*): keep the search on the fast solver, and spend the slow solver
**once**, at the end, confirming the winner — not on every candidate.

**Concrete mechanism:**

1. **Leave `SIM_SOLVER` pointed at the bundled fast oracle** (default
   `app.sim.oracle:solve`, or the sim team's PyNEC cross-check once it's
   installable — see `rf/progress_simulation.md`'s PyNEC/MSVC note) for the
   whole agent loop. The agent keeps searching broadly and cheaply, exactly
   as already verified in M0/M2.
2. **Add a new, separate env**, e.g. `CONFIRM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve`
   (unset by default — opt-in, since it needs `rf/.venv` present).
3. **Add one `pool.solve_with(solver_spec, spec, band, cand)` function**
   (small addition to `app/sim/pool.py`) that resolves and runs a solver by
   name **on demand**, instead of always reading the process-wide
   `SIM_SOLVER` env — everything else about the process pool (isolation,
   async dispatch) stays the same.
4. **In `orchestrator._finish()`** (`app/runs/orchestrator.py`), after the
   `ranking` is decided but before `run_finished` is emitted: if
   `CONFIRM_SOLVER` is set and a winner exists, call
   `pool.solve_with(CONFIRM_SOLVER, run.spec, band_for(run, winner), winner)`
   with a **generous, separate timeout** (real FDTD minutes, not the
   interactive loop's budget — this call is off the critical path, it's the
   very last thing before reporting). Attach the result as a new artifact,
   e.g. `openems_confirmation`, alongside the existing `agent_report`
   addendum — **never a gate**: if it fails (no `rf/.venv` on this machine,
   openEMS crash, timeout), the run still finishes with the oracle-based
   ranking and simply notes the confirmation didn't run, mirroring exactly
   how `agent_report` already degrades today.
5. This gives you, honestly, both things the user is asking for at once:
   the agent still autonomously walks the whole candidate space the way an
   RF engineer would (fast oracle, in-loop, already proven), *and* the
   headline number that ships in the report is checked against the real
   physics-accurate FDTD solver (slow, but only paid once per run).

If, instead, the actual intent is *"I want the agent's in-loop reasoning to
be based on real FDTD numbers, not the oracle's,"* that's a different,
harder ask — it means shrinking the anchor grid drastically (e.g. corners
only, no edge points) and accepting a much shallower search per run. Worth
an explicit decision before building; the confirmation-step approach above
is the one that doesn't force that trade-off. Flag which one is wanted
before §8 starts.

## 7. Where to place new engineering rules

A recurring question as this gets built out further: when a new placement or
antenna-design rule comes up, where does it belong? The codebase already
draws this line in a few places — worth keeping consistent rather than
picking ad hoc per rule:

| Kind of rule | Example | Lives in | Why there |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hard physical/geometric constraint** — not a judgment call, either it's buildable/correct or it isn't | IFA arm must run beside the ground plane, not above it (image-current cancellation); arm direction derived from board interior, not the raw feed/short offset | `rf/geometry.py` (what the solver is even allowed to construct) | Enforced deterministically at the geometry-building layer; never left to the agent or the LLM to get right by accident |
| **Candidate-position search space** — which spots exist to be proposed at all | perimeter anchors, corner-first, spacing_mm | `app/geometry/spec.py::make_anchors()` | This *is* the "candidate generation layer" (deep-research §5); device-derived, computed once per spec, not per-run config |
| **Hard pre-screen / keep-out check** — reject a spot before ever simulating it | distance to nearest metal ≥ band's `clearance_mm` | `app/geometry/spec.py::clearance_at()`, consumed by both anchor annotation and `score.py` diffs | Cheap, deterministic, geometry-only — no need to burn a simulation to learn this |
| **Deterministic engineering hint** — arithmetic diagnosis of a completed simulation | "resonance 2.62 GHz vs 2.44 → arm ~7% short"; "R=18Ω too low → increase gap_mm" | `app/sim/score.py::hints_for()` | Explicit design principle already in the code's own docstring: *"Hints are deterministic physics arithmetic — never LLM."* Keep it that way; a new hint is a new `if` branch here, not prompt text |
| **Narrative rule of thumb** — background knowledge the agent should keep in mind while reasoning, not a computed fact about one candidate | "λ/4 monopole rarely fits a phone edge — prefer IFA/meander"; "corners clear in two directions" | `app/agent/prompts.py::ANTENNA_NOTES` | This is the free-text "playbook" injected into the create prompt — advisory, not gated; the right place for anything you'd say out loud to a junior RF engineer once, not check in code |
| **Convergence / stopping policy** — when is a design "good enough" | how many iterations, when to stop refining | Nowhere in the backend, deliberately — the agent's own judgment (ADR-5) | *"Agent decides convergence; orchestrator enforces only the simulation gate"* — a deliberate architecture decision (DESIGN.md ADR-5), not an oversight. Do not add a `max_iterations` here without revisiting that ADR first |
| **Which solver runs when** (fast search vs. slow confirmation) | oracle for search, real FDTD once at the end | `SIM_SOLVER` / `CONFIRM_SOLVER` env selection + `orchestrator._finish()` (see §6, new) | Budget-driven infrastructure choice, not engineering judgment — the backend should own it outright, the agent shouldn't need to reason about which solver it's talking to |

Rule of thumb for a new rule you're adding: **"is this true regardless of
which candidate we're looking at, or computed from one candidate's
result?"** — the former goes in `spec.py`/`geometry.py` (search-space /
hard-constraint layer), the latter in `score.py` (per-result hints) unless
it's genuinely advisory background knowledge, in which case it goes in
`prompts.py::ANTENNA_NOTES` as prose for the agent to reason with.

## 8. Step-by-step plan

1. **Decide search strategy up front** (§6): two-tier (fast search + one
   real-solver confirmation, recommended) vs. real-solver-in-the-loop
   (shallow search, simpler code, much longer/rarer runs). Everything below
   assumes the two-tier approach; skip 6b/6c if the other is chosen instead.

2. **Add a real CLI entrypoint to `rf/`.** `rf/run_simulation.py`'s
   `if __name__ == "__main__":` block currently only runs a hardcoded demo
   config — it does not read a config path from `sys.argv`, despite both
   `rf/README.md` and `progress_simulation.md` step 8 describing
   `python -m rf.run_simulation config.json` as the intended CLI. This needs
   a small addition before anything can shell out to it — either:
   - extend the existing `__main__` block to accept an optional
     `sys.argv[1]` config path (falls back to the demo when absent), or
   - add a tiny separate `rf/cli.py` (stdin JSON in → stdout JSON out, no new
     dependencies) so the demo `__main__` stays untouched.
   Flag this to the sim team — it's their file, one-line-ish change, but
   blocks step 3 until it exists.

3. **Replace the in-process import in `rf_adapter.solve()` with a subprocess
   call**, mirroring `app/geometry/extract.py`'s `_command()` pattern:
   - Resolve the interpreter: `RF_PYTHON` env var override, else default to
     `<repo_root>/rf/.venv/Scripts/python.exe` (this repo is Windows-only for
     the openEMS wheels anyway); error clearly if it doesn't exist.
   - `subprocess.run([rf_python, "-m", "rf.cli"], cwd=repo_root, input=json.dumps(cfg), capture_output=True, timeout=RF_TIMEOUT_S)`
     — `cwd=repo_root` matters, same reason as `rf/README.md`'s "always
     `python -m rf.<module>`, never direct" rule (relative imports need
     package context).
   - Parse stdout as JSON → existing `from_result()` unchanged.
   - Non-zero exit / timeout / missing interpreter → `SimResult(status="failed", notes=...)`,
     same fail-soft pattern already in the file (never crash a candidate's slot).

4. **Add `pool.solve_with()` and the `CONFIRM_SOLVER` finish-time call**
   (§6, steps 3-4) — small, additive; nothing existing changes shape.

5. **Confirm the device-manifest path lines up end to end.** When a run goes
   through `/devices` (real `.blend` ingest), `classify.py` sets
   `DeviceSpec.geometry_path` to `<device_dir>/out/geometry.json`;
   `rf_adapter.build_config()` forwards that as `device.manifest_path`;
   `rf.device.load_device()` reads it as plain JSON (no `bpy`, by design).
   Spot-check that the field names match exactly (`parts[].{node_path,
   material_key, eps_r, sigma_S_per_m, bbox_mm, stl_path}`) — DESIGN.md §8
   already asserts `geometry.json` is a superset of rf's own manifest shape,
   but this has not been run for real yet.

6. **Test in four widening steps, each gated on the previous passing:**
   1. **Adapter-only, real solver, canned spec, single candidate:**
      `RF_TIMEOUT_S=300 uv run python -c "..."` calling `rf_adapter.solve()`
      directly against `phone_v1()` — confirms the subprocess call itself
      works and returns a real (not stubbed) S11 curve.
   2. **Real device asset, adapter-only:**
      same, but `DeviceSpec.geometry_path` pointed at
      `data/apple_iphone_15_pro/.../geometry.json` — confirms
      `manifest_path` → real bbox materials flow through to an actual FDTD
      solve, not just the bare board.
   3. **Full loop with confirmation, mock agent:**
      `AGENT=mock CONFIRM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve uv run python scripts/dev_run.py`
      — oracle-driven search runs exactly as before (fast), then the one
      extra real-solver confirmation call fires at the end; check the
      `openems_confirmation` artifact lands and that a missing/broken
      `rf/.venv` degrades gracefully rather than failing the run.
   4. **Live Devin run**, only once 1-3 are green: `AGENT=devin`, same
      fixtures, watching that the confirmation step doesn't blow past a
      reasonable extra wait after `run_finished` would otherwise fire.
   Add an **opt-in** integration test (e.g.
   `backend/scripts/rf_integration_test.py`) that auto-skips when
   `rf/.venv` isn't present, so this never blocks anyone without the
   openEMS setup — the existing `selftest.py` stays stub-only and fast.

7. **Update docs once verified:** `backend/README.md` "Seams" section and
   `rf/README.md` "Status" currently describe this as untested
   ("...against their real solver only once it runs on a shared machine").
   Replace with the actual first real timing/result once §8 passes, and
   record whether the confirmation step (§6) agreed with the oracle's
   ranking or flagged a mismatch worth investigating.

## 9. Open risks to flag explicitly

- **rf's own resonance numbers are not yet validated** (tutorial cross-check
  and PyNEC cross-check are both still open per
  `rf/progress_simulation.md`). Wiring the plumbing correctly does not by
  itself make the confirmation step's numbers physically trustworthy — that's
  a separate, pre-existing gap in the sim workstream. If the real-solver
  confirmation disagrees sharply with the oracle's ranking, that's as likely
  to be rf's own unvalidated resonance as a wiring bug — don't assume the
  adapter is broken before checking `rf/progress_simulation.md`'s open items.
- **Windows-only.** openEMS's prebuilt wheels are MSVC/`win_amd64`; this
  whole path only works on a Windows machine with `rf/.venv` set up per
  `rf/README.md`. Worth stating plainly in `backend/README.md` as a
  requirement for whoever flips `SIM_SOLVER`/`CONFIRM_SOLVER`.
- **`rf/cli.py` (or the `__main__` change) is the sim team's file** — raise
  it with them rather than unilaterally changing their entrypoint; keeps
  "one code path" ownership clean the same way `tools/extract_blend.py` is
  shared but singly-owned.
- **Two-tier search-then-confirm (§6) means the agent's in-loop reasoning
  never sees real FDTD numbers**, only the oracle's. If a stakeholder's
  expectation is "Devin reasons over real openEMS results the whole time,"
  say so explicitly — that's the harder, slower alternative named in §6,
  and it's a scope decision, not an implementation detail.

## Proposed concrete file changes (for when this plan is approved)

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `rf/cli.py` (new) or `rf/run_simulation.py` | accept a JSON config via stdin/argv, print result JSON to stdout |
| `backend/app/sim/rf_adapter.py` | subprocess dispatch to `RF_PYTHON` instead of in-process import |
| `backend/app/sim/pool.py` | add `solve_with(solver_spec, spec, band, cand)` for on-demand solver selection (§6) |
| `backend/app/runs/orchestrator.py` | `_finish()`: optional `CONFIRM_SOLVER` real-solver confirmation call on the winner, addendum artifact only (§6) |
| `backend/scripts/rf_integration_test.py` (new) | opt-in real-solver smoke test, skips if `rf/.venv` absent |
| `backend/README.md`, `rf/README.md` | status update once §8 is verified; document the two-tier solver strategy |
| `.env.example` / README env docs | document `RF_PYTHON`, `RF_TIMEOUT_S`, `CONFIRM_SOLVER` |

"""Thin CLI wrapper around run_simulation(), for callers that can't import
this package in-process (the FastAPI backend runs Python 3.12; openEMS/CSXCAD
are Python 3.11-only wheels installed in rf/.venv — see rf/README.md Setup).
Those callers shell out to rf/.venv's interpreter instead
(backend/app/sim/rf_adapter.py does exactly this).

Reads one config dict as JSON from stdin, writes the SimResult dict as JSON
to stdout. Never raises past main() -- an exception is reported as a
"failed"-status result on stdout so the caller always gets parseable JSON
back, exit code 0 either way; a non-zero exit means stdin/stdout itself
couldn't be read/written.

    python -m rf.cli < config.json > result.json

Run as `python -m rf.cli` from the repo root -- relative imports need
package context, same rule as every other rf/ module (see rf/README.md).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

"""Adapter from our solver seam to the sim workstream's entry point.

Their contract (rf/run_simulation.py, branch feat/simulation):

    run_simulation(config: dict) -> dict          # SimResult-shaped
    config = {"candidate": {...}, "band": {...}, "device": {...}, "sim": {...}}

Select it with  SIM_SOLVER=app.sim.rf_adapter:solve . Nothing else in the
backend changes: this module runs inside the process pool like any solver.

**Cross-venv, not in-process.** openEMS/CSXCAD are Windows wheels built for
Python 3.11, installed only in rf/.venv (rf/README.md Setup); the backend
itself runs Python 3.12 (backend/pyproject.toml). `from rf.run_simulation
import run_simulation` would raise ModuleNotFoundError the instant this ran
inside the backend's own interpreter (in the ProcessPoolExecutor, that's the
same interpreter as the parent process) -- there is no way to install
openEMS into the backend's venv without an ABI mismatch. So `solve()` below
shells out to rf/.venv's python via `rf/cli.py` (stdin JSON in, stdout JSON
out), the exact pattern `app/geometry/extract.py` already uses for the
bpy/Python-3.11 boundary.

Mapping notes (keep in sync with rf/models.py):
- their Candidate dataclass rejects unknown keys -> only the types.ts fields
  are forwarded (anchor_id / band_id / prior / rationale / params stay here).
- their IFA builder reads the pin height from feed_point_mm.z (0 -> default),
  so our `params.height_mm` is mapped onto it.
- `device.manifest_path` -> the device's geometry.json (same manifest shape
  their blend_loader writes: parts[].{node_path, material_key, eps_r,
  sigma_S_per_m, bbox_mm, stl_path}); `device.board.size_mm` is the device
  outline; `device.components` is our classified list for when their step 6
  (real materials) lands.
- their result has no input impedance -> ours stays (0, 0) and the scorer
  skips the impedance hints.
- `SIM_OPTS` env (JSON) passes solver knobs, e.g.
  {"mesh_res": "coarse", "boundary": "MUR", "freq_points": 21}.

Env: `RF_PYTHON` overrides the interpreter (default: `rf/.venv/Scripts/python.exe`
on Windows, `rf/.venv/bin/python` elsewhere); `RF_TIMEOUT_S` overrides the
subprocess timeout (default 600s -- FDTD solves run minutes, not the
oracle's milliseconds).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import subprocess
import time
from pathlib import Path

from app.models import BandRequirement, Candidate, DeviceSpec, S11Point, SimResult

REPO_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_S = 600.0


def _rf_python() -> Path | None:
    """Resolve an openEMS-capable interpreter. Never assumes -- returns None
    (not a guess) if nothing is found, so the caller can fail with a clear
    message instead of a confusing ModuleNotFoundError two layers down."""
    if py := os.environ.get("RF_PYTHON"):
        p = Path(py)
        return p if p.exists() else None
    for candidate in (REPO_DIR / "rf" / ".venv" / "Scripts" / "python.exe",  # Windows
                     REPO_DIR / "rf" / ".venv" / "bin" / "python"):          # posix
        if candidate.exists():
            return candidate
    return None

def test_rf_adapter() -> None:
    spec = phone_v1()
    band = spec.requirements.bands[0]
    cand = Candidate(candidate_id="a1", anchor_id="c_bl", band_id="wifi24",
                     antenna_type="IFA", position_mm=(6, 6, 5.5), feed_point_mm=(6, 6, 5.5),
                     length_mm=30.0, orientation="corner", params={"height_mm": 3.0, "gap_mm": 5})
    cfg = rf_adapter.build_config(spec, band, cand)
    assert set(cfg["candidate"]) == {"candidate_id", "antenna_type", "position_mm",
                                     "feed_point_mm", "length_mm", "orientation"}
    assert cfg["candidate"]["feed_point_mm"][2] == 3.0 and cfg["band"]["id"] == "wifi24"
    assert "manifest_path" not in cfg["device"] and cfg["device"]["board"]["size_mm"]

    # solve() shells out to rf/.venv's interpreter (rf.cli, stdin/stdout JSON) --
    # openEMS is Python-3.11-only, this process is 3.12 (see rf_adapter's
    # module docstring). Stub subprocess.run itself rather than importing rf.
    stub_out = {
        "candidate_id": cand.candidate_id, "status": "complete", "runtime_s": 12.5,
        "s11_curve": [{"f_ghz": 2.4, "s11_db": -9.0}, {"f_ghz": 2.44, "s11_db": -15.0}],
        "s11_min_db": -15.0, "resonant_ghz": 2.44, "bandwidth_mhz": 80.0, "efficiency": 0.6,
        "peak_gain_dbi": 1.5, "vswr": 1.4, "sar_w_per_kg": 0.0, "meets_requirements": True,
        "notes": "stub"}

    real_run, real_rf_python = rf_adapter.subprocess.run, rf_adapter._rf_python
    rf_adapter._rf_python = lambda: pathlib.Path("stub-python")
    try:
        rf_adapter.subprocess.run = lambda *a, **k: types.SimpleNamespace(
            returncode=0, stdout=json.dumps(stub_out), stderr="")
        r = rf_adapter.solve(spec, band, cand)
        assert r.status == "complete" and r.s11_min_db == -15.0 and r.impedance_ohm == (0.0, 0.0)
        assert not any("radiation resistance" in h for h in hints_for(spec, band, cand, r))

        rf_adapter.subprocess.run = lambda *a, **k: types.SimpleNamespace(
            returncode=1, stdout="", stderr="ImportError: no module named CSXCAD")
        r = rf_adapter.solve(spec, band, cand)
        assert r.status == "failed" and "ImportError" in r.notes

        def boom(*a, **k):
            raise rf_adapter.subprocess.TimeoutExpired(cmd="rf.cli", timeout=1)
        rf_adapter.subprocess.run = boom
        r = rf_adapter.solve(spec, band, cand)
        assert r.status == "failed" and "timed out" in r.notes
    finally:
        rf_adapter.subprocess.run, rf_adapter._rf_python = real_run, real_rf_python

    rf_adapter._rf_python = lambda: None
    try:
        r = rf_adapter.solve(spec, band, cand)
        assert r.status == "failed" and "rf/.venv not found" in r.notes
    finally:
        rf_adapter._rf_python = real_rf_python
    print("ok  rf_adapter mapping + subprocess dispatch + failure paths")

"""Thin CLI wrapper around run_simulation(), for callers that can't import
this package in-process (the FastAPI backend runs Python 3.12; openEMS/CSXCAD
are Python 3.11-only wheels installed in rf/.venv — see rf/README.md Setup).
Those callers shell out to rf/.venv's interpreter instead
(backend/app/sim/rf_adapter.py does exactly this).

Reads one config dict as JSON from stdin, writes the SimResult dict as JSON
to the file at --out. **Not stdout** -- openEMS's C++ engine writes its own
verbose progress logging directly to the process's stdout (confirmed live:
running this against a real config interleaves "openEMS 64bit -- version
..." / per-timestep energy lines with whatever this script prints), so a
JSON result on stdout is not reliably parseable. Same problem, same fix as
tools/extract_blend.py already uses for bpy's console spam: write the
result to a file, don't rely on stdout for structured data.

    python -m rf.cli --out result.json < config.json

Exit code is always 0 if stdin/the config were readable at all -- a failure
inside run_simulation() (including "no openEMS on this machine") is reported
as a normal "failed"-status result written to --out, not a crash, so the
caller always gets one parseable file back. A non-zero exit / no output file
means something more fundamental broke (bad --out path, stdin unreadable).

Run as `python -m rf.cli` from the repo root -- relative imports need
package context, same rule as every other rf/ module (see rf/README.md).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys

from .run_simulation import run_simulation


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--out", required=True, help="path to write the result JSON to")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    config: dict = {}
    try:
        config = json.loads(sys.stdin.read())
        result = run_simulation(config)
    except Exception as e:
        result = {
            "candidate_id": config.get("candidate", {}).get("candidate_id", ""),
            "status": "failed", "runtime_s": 0.0, "s11_curve": [], "s11_min_db": 0.0,
            "resonant_ghz": 0.0, "bandwidth_mhz": 0.0, "efficiency": 0.0,
            "peak_gain_dbi": 0.0, "vswr": 0.0, "sar_w_per_kg": 0.0,
            "meets_requirements": False,
            "notes": f"rf.cli error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}",
        }
    with open(args.out, "w") as f:
        json.dump(result, f)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

async def solve_async(spec: DeviceSpec, band: BandRequirement,
                      cand: Candidate) -> SimResult:
    """Solve one candidate with whatever SIM_SOLVER names (the process-wide
    default -- the in-loop search)."""
    return await _run(spec, band, cand, None)


async def solve_with(solver_spec: str, spec: DeviceSpec, band: BandRequirement,
                     cand: Candidate) -> SimResult:
    """Solve one candidate with an EXPLICIT solver, bypassing SIM_SOLVER --
    e.g. a one-off real-FDTD confirmation of the agent's winner after a
    fast-oracle search concludes (integration plan §6: the in-loop search
    stays cheap; the real solver is spent once, on the result that's about
    to ship). Same process pool, same isolation/crash containment as the
    regular search path."""
    return await _run(spec, band, cand, solver_spec)


async def _run(spec: DeviceSpec, band: BandRequirement, cand: Candidate,
               solver_spec: str | None) -> SimResult:
    assert _pool is not None, "pool not started"
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    try:
        raw = await loop.run_in_executor(
            _pool, _worker, spec.model_dump_json(), band.model_dump_json(),
            cand.model_dump_json(), solver_spec)
        return SimResult.model_validate_json(raw)
    except Exception as e:  # BrokenProcessPool et al.
        return SimResult(candidate_id=cand.candidate_id, status="failed",
                         notes=f"pool failure: {e}")

async def _confirm_winner(run: Run, best: str) -> None:
    """One real-solver confirmation of the agent's already-decided winner
    (integration plan §6) -- runs after run_finished, never before: it must
    never gate or slow down the in-loop search, only add evidence to the
    report. Failure (no rf/.venv on this machine, solver crash/timeout)
    degrades to a note in the artifact, the same way a missing agent_report
    degrades today -- it is never allowed to fail the run."""
    cand = run.candidates[best]
    run.log.emit("report", EventType.decision, {
        "decision": f"confirming winner {best!r} against CONFIRM_SOLVER={CONFIRM_SOLVER}"})
    result = await pool.solve_with(CONFIRM_SOLVER, run.spec, band_for(run, cand), cand)
